claim: Mice with distinct cognitive experiences use different cortical areas to solve the same navigation decision task.
source: We discovered that mice with distinct cognitive experiences, beyond sensory and motor learning, use different cortical areas and neural activity patterns to solve the same navigation decision task, revealing past learning as a critical determinant of whether cortex is necessary for goal-directed navigation.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Past learning is a critical determinant of whether cortex is necessary for goal-directed navigation.
source: We discovered that mice with distinct cognitive experiences, beyond sensory and motor learning, use different cortical areas and neural activity patterns to solve the same navigation decision task, revealing past learning as a critical determinant of whether cortex is necessary for goal-directed navigation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental findings showing differential cortical necessity based on training history.

claim: Posterior parietal cortex and retrosplenial cortex were mostly dispensable for accurate performance of a simple navigation task in mice without complex-task experience.
source: Posterior parietal cortex and retrosplenial cortex were mostly dispensable for accurate performance of a simple navigation task.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition data showing minimal performance deficits.

claim: PPC and RSC were essential for the simple task when mice were previously trained on complex tasks with delay periods or association switches.
source: In contrast, these areas were essential for the same simple task when mice were previously trained on complex tasks with delay periods or association switches.
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic inhibition experiments showing large performance deficits in mice with complex-task experience.

claim: In mice with complex-task experience, single-neuron activity had higher selectivity during the simple task.
source: Multiarea calcium imaging showed that, in mice with complex-task experience, single-neuron activity had higher selectivity and neuron–neuron correlations were weaker, leading to codes with higher task information.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing neural activity patterns across training histories.

claim: In mice with complex-task experience, neuron–neuron correlations were weaker during the simple task.
source: Multiarea calcium imaging showed that, in mice with complex-task experience, single-neuron activity had higher selectivity and neuron–neuron correlations were weaker, leading to codes with higher task information.
evidence: This is demonstrated by noise correlation analyses from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Higher selectivity and weaker correlations lead to codes with higher task information.
source: Multiarea calcium imaging showed that, in mice with complex-task experience, single-neuron activity had higher selectivity and neuron–neuron correlations were weaker, leading to codes with higher task information.
evidence: This is supported by decoding analyses showing improved trial-type decoding accuracy.

claim: Past experience is a key factor in determining whether cortical areas have a causal role in goal-directed navigation.
source: Therefore, past experience is a key factor in determining whether cortical areas have a causal role in goal-directed navigation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined optogenetic and imaging experiments.

claim: The necessity of cortical areas has been tested during tasks that involve different sensory, behavioral, and cognitive features across studies.
source: Across studies, the necessity of cortical areas has been tested during tasks that involve different sensory, behavioral, and cognitive features (Ceballo et al., 2019; Erlich et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2020; Goard et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2014; Harvey et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2018; Licata et al., 2017; Raposo et al., 2014; Yang and Zador, 2012; Zhou and Freedman, 2019; Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: In rodents, posterior parietal cortex is necessary for visual but not some auditory discrimination tasks.
source: For example, in rodents, posterior parietal cortex (PPC) is necessary for visual but not some auditory discrimination tasks (Licata et al., 2017) and is considered to be especially involved in tasks that have a short-term memory component, such as a delay period between sensory cues and choice reports, or a requirement for evidence accumulation over time (Lyamzin and Benucci, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Licata et al., 2017.

claim: PPC is considered to be especially involved in tasks that have a short-term memory component.
source: For example, in rodents, posterior parietal cortex (PPC) is necessary for visual but not some auditory discrimination tasks (Licata et al., 2017) and is considered to be especially involved in tasks that have a short-term memory component, such as a delay period between sensory cues and choice reports, or a requirement for evidence accumulation over time (Lyamzin and Benucci, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lyamzin and Benucci, 2019.

claim: Area LIP in monkeys is thought to be essential for sensory but not motor aspects of visual motion discrimination tasks.
source: As another example, area LIP in monkeys is thought to be essential for sensory but not motor aspects of visual motion discrimination tasks (Zhou and Freedman, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou and Freedman, 2019.

claim: Most studies have not investigated the effect of past learning on the involvement of cortex.
source: Although it is intuitive that past learning, beyond the demands of the task-of-interest, may impact how individuals perform decision tasks, most studies have not investigated the effect of past learning on the involvement of cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on literature review.

claim: For coarse depth discrimination, MT was only necessary in monkeys that had no prior experience in fine depth discrimination tasks.
source: For coarse depth discrimination, MT was only necessary in monkeys that had no prior experience in fine depth discrimination tasks (Chowdhury and DeAngelis, 2008), showing a decrease in cortical involvement with additional experience.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chowdhury and DeAngelis, 2008.

claim: For motion discrimination, previous training on moving dot stimuli rendered MT necessary for discriminating the motion of gratings.
source: In contrast, for motion discrimination, previous training on moving dot stimuli rendered MT necessary for discriminating the motion of gratings (Liu and Pack, 2017), showing that sensory experience can also increase cortical involvement.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu and Pack, 2017.

claim: Studies of motor learning have shown that cortex is essential during the learning process but becomes dispensable after learning is completed.
source: Relatedly, studies of motor learning have shown that cortex is essential during the learning process but becomes dispensable after learning is completed (Hwang et al., 2019; Kawai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hwang et al., 2019 and Kawai et al., 2015.

claim: Movement through virtual mazes is known to recruit navigation-related circuits.
source: Furthermore, it involves navigation because mice must execute a sequence of movements to reach a goal location in a virtual environment, and movement through virtual mazes is known to recruit navigation-related circuits (Aronov and Tank, 2014; Domnisoru et al., 2013; Harvey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aronov and Tank, 2014; Domnisoru et al., 2013; Harvey et al., 2009.

claim: PPC has been studied extensively in the context of decision-making across species.
source: PPC has been studied extensively in the context of decision-making across species and is generally thought to convert sensory cues into motor plans (Freedman and Ibos, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Freedman and Ibos, 2018.

claim: PPC is generally thought to convert sensory cues into motor plans.
source: PPC has been studied extensively in the context of decision-making across species and is generally thought to convert sensory cues into motor plans (Freedman and Ibos, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Freedman and Ibos, 2018.

claim: RSC is considered to be critical for reference frame transformations underlying basic navigation.
source: PPC is strongly interconnected with RSC, which is considered to be critical for reference frame transformations underlying basic navigation and to support spatial memory across various timescales (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2015; Fischer et al., 2020; Milczarek et al., 2018; Pothuizen et al., 2009; Powell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2015; Fischer et al., 2020; Milczarek et al., 2018; Pothuizen et al., 2009; Powell et al., 2017.

claim: RSC supports spatial memory across various timescales.
source: PPC is strongly interconnected with RSC, which is considered to be critical for reference frame transformations underlying basic navigation and to support spatial memory across various timescales (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2015; Fischer et al., 2020; Milczarek et al., 2018; Pothuizen et al., 2009; Powell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2015; Fischer et al., 2020; Milczarek et al., 2018; Pothuizen et al., 2009; Powell et al., 2017.

claim: RSC is involved in cognitive processes beyond spatial navigation, such as context-dependent cue–choice associations, temporal learning, and value coding.
source: RSC is furthermore involved in cognitive processes beyond spatial navigation, such as context-dependent cue–choice associations, temporal learning, and value coding (Franco and Goard, 2021; Hattori et al., 2019; Todd et al., 2015), making it an especially interesting area to study in the context of cognitive experience.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Franco and Goard, 2021; Hattori et al., 2019; Todd et al., 2015.

claim: Silencing S1 did not affect performance in the simple task.
source: Silencing S1 did not affect performance, and inhibition of PPC resulted in a very small performance decrease, with mean performance of 90 ± 2% correct (mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM]).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Inhibition of PPC resulted in a very small performance decrease in the simple task, with mean performance of 90 ± 2% correct.
source: Silencing S1 did not affect performance, and inhibition of PPC resulted in a very small performance decrease, with mean performance of 90 ± 2% correct (mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM]).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Inhibition of RSC resulted in intermediate performance levels of 77 ± 3% correct in the simple task.
source: Inhibition of RSC had the largest effect, resulting in intermediate performance levels of 77 ± 3% correct.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mice still performed well above chance (50% correct) with RSC inhibited in the simple task.
source: However, mice still performed well above chance (50% correct).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Effects of RSC inhibition on performance were similar in the simple task and the run-to-target task.
source: Effects on performance were similar in this run-to-target task, suggesting that RSC inhibition in the simple task may impair lower-level processes such as basic navigation instead of decision-making based on cue–choice associations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of inhibition effects across tasks shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: S1 inhibition during the complex tasks caused a modest decrease in performance, but mice still performed the tasks at high levels.
source: S1 inhibition during the complex tasks caused a modest decrease in performance, but mice still performed the tasks at high levels (Figure 1F, H).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figures 1F and 1H.

claim: Inhibition of PPC or RSC greatly impaired performance in the delay and switching tasks and resulted in performance of 55 ± 3% correct, which is close to chance levels.
source: In contrast, inhibition of PPC or RSC greatly impaired performance in the delay and switching tasks and resulted in performance of 55 ± 3% correct, which is close to chance levels.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figures 1F and 1H.

claim: The effects of inhibiting PPC and RSC were markedly larger in the delay and switching tasks than in the simple task.
source: The effects of inhibiting PPC and RSC were markedly larger in the delay and switching tasks than in the simple task (Figure 1I, J).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of inhibition effects shown in Figures 1I and 1J.

claim: Adding a delay epoch to the trial or frequent association switches across trials increased the necessity of cortex relative to the simple task.
source: Therefore, adding a delay epoch to the trial or frequent association switches across trials increased the necessity of cortex relative to the simple task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of inhibition effects across tasks.

claim: Inhibition of PPC or RSC in both the cue and delay segments decreased performance to a greater degree than in the simple task.
source: Inhibition of PPC or RSC in both trial segments decreased performance to a greater degree than in the simple task, indicating that PPC and RSC are necessary for multiple epochs of the task.
evidence: This is supported by segment-specific inhibition data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The effects of inhibition were restricted to the current trial, as inhibition did not affect subsequent control trials.
source: Taking advantage of interleaved control and inhibition trials, we found that the effects of inhibition were restricted to the current trial, as inhibition did not affect subsequent control trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of control trials following inhibition trials shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: PPC inhibition during the intertrial interval did not affect the recovery of performance after a rule switch.
source: We silenced PPC during the intertrial interval on every trial following a rule switch, for 50 consecutive trials. However, PPC inhibition did not affect the recovery of performance after a rule switch (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by ITI inhibition data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The increased necessity of PPC and RSC during the delay and switching tasks did not appear to be specific to the added task components.
source: Thus, the increased necessity of PPC and RSC during the delay and switching tasks did not appear to be specific to the added task components.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the segment-specific and ITI inhibition experiments.

claim: Relative to the simple task, it took mice longer to become experts at the delay and switching tasks.
source: We verified that the complex tasks were indeed more challenging for mice. Relative to the simple task, it took mice longer to become experts at the delay and switching tasks (Methods), and their performance on control trials was lower (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by training time data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Performance on control trials was lower in the delay and switching tasks compared to the simple task.
source: We verified that the complex tasks were indeed more challenging for mice. Relative to the simple task, it took mice longer to become experts at the delay and switching tasks (Methods), and their performance on control trials was lower (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by performance data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: In mice with previous delay task experience, inhibition of PPC and RSC during the simple task greatly impaired behavioral performance to 67 ± 3% and 62 ± 2% correct, respectively.
source: In these mice, inhibition of PPC and RSC during the simple task greatly impaired behavioral performance to 67 ± 3% and 62 ± 2% correct (mean ± SEM), respectively (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Mice with previous delay task experience needed PPC and RSC activity to perform at high levels on the simple task.
source: Thus, these mice needed PPC and RSC activity to perform at high levels on the simple task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inhibition data in mice with delay task experience.

claim: The larger effect of PPC and RSC inhibition due to previous delay task experience persisted for the full 2 weeks that was investigated.
source: The larger effect of PPC and RSC inhibition due to previous delay task experience was not only apparent immediately after the transition to the simple task but persisted for the full 2 weeks that we investigated (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal inhibition data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Mice with distinct previous task experience require different cortical areas to perform the same task.
source: Thus, mice with distinct previous task experience require different cortical areas to perform the same task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing inhibition effects across training histories.

claim: Mice with delay task experience performed at very high levels on trials without laser light even in the first session after the transition to the simple task.
source: However, these mice performed at very high levels on trials without laser light even in the first session after the transition to the simple task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral performance data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Performance on control trials in the simple task was as high in mice with delay task experience as in mice with simple task experience only.
source: Relatedly, performance on control trials in the simple task was as high in mice with delay task experience as in mice with simple task experience only, indicating that subjective task difficulty did not differ depending on training history (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by performance comparison data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In mice with previous switching task experience, PPC and RSC inhibition resulted in performance of 67 ± 3% and 61 ± 3% correct, respectively, on the simple task.
source: In mice that had previously been experts on the switching task, PPC and RSC inhibition resulted in performance of 67 ± 3% and 61 ± 3% correct (mean ± SEM), respectively, on the simple task (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: PPC activity was necessary even 2 weeks after the transition to the simple task in mice with switching task experience.
source: As for previous training on the delay task, this effect of PPC and RSC inhibition during the simple task was markedly larger than when these areas were inhibited in mice without previous training on the switching task (Figure 3D, E). PPC activity was necessary even 2 weeks after the transition to the simple task.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal inhibition data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: RSC's involvement was greatest in the first week after the transition to the simple task in mice with switching task experience.
source: RSC's involvement was greatest in the first week after the transition.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal inhibition data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Mice with previous experience in the switching task require PPC and RSC activity to perform the simple task.
source: Therefore, mice with previous experience in the switching task require PPC and RSC activity to perform the simple task, whereas these areas are largely dispensable during performance of the same simple task in mice without this previous training.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing inhibition effects across training histories.

claim: Previous experience in complex tasks did not make cortex essential for all simple tasks.
source: Notably, inhibition of PPC and RSC during the run-to-target task resulted in similarly minor performance drops in groups of mice with and without prior complex-task experience (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Thus, previous experience in complex tasks did not make cortex essential for all simple tasks.
evidence: This is supported by run-to-target task inhibition data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Past experience is a key factor in determining whether cortical areas have a causal role in goal-directed navigation.
source: Collectively, these results highlight that the cortical areas used to perform a task can be profoundly shaped by experience from weeks ago. Mice with different previous task experience use distinct sets of cortical areas to solve the same task. Therefore, an understanding of which areas of cortex are necessary for decision tasks requires considering both the demands of the task-of-interest and the previous experiences of the individual.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Neurons in RSC and PPC had higher activity in the switching task than in the simple task.
source: Interestingly, this basic measure revealed differences across tasks, as neurons in RSC and PPC had higher activity in the switching task than in the simple task (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PPC and RSC neurons showed higher average levels of trial-type selectivity in the switching task than in the simple task.
source: PPC and RSC neurons showed higher average levels of trial-type selectivity in the switching task than in the simple task (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The fraction of RSC or PPC neurons with significant trial-type selectivity was higher in the switching task than in the simple task.
source: In addition, the fraction of RSC or PPC neurons with significant trial-type selectivity was higher in the switching task than in the simple task (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: For the same size population in the switching task, decoding accuracy in RSC and PPC was higher than in the simple task.
source: However, for the same size population in the switching task, this decoding accuracy in RSC and PPC was even higher, in line with the observed increased selectivity and larger fraction of selective neurons relative to the simple task (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: V1 neurons had similar levels of activity, selectivity, and population-level trial-type decoding in the simple and switching tasks.
source: In contrast, V1 neurons had similar levels of activity, selectivity, and population-level trial-type decoding in the simple and switching tasks (Figure 4D–H).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 4D-H.

claim: The differences in neural selectivity cannot be trivially explained by differences in running patterns.
source: We verified that the differences in selectivity across tasks were not due to differences in running patterns. When we selected sessions so that the time course and magnitude of decoding the mouse's reported choice from its running were similar across tasks, we largely observed the same differences in neural trial-type selectivity as reported above (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Thus, the differences in neural selectivity cannot be trivially explained by differences in running patterns.
evidence: This is supported by analysis controlling for running patterns shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A large fraction of neurons in all imaged areas, but highest in RSC, showed increased activity specifically for a single trial type in the switching task.
source: By examining single-neuron activity across all four trial types, that is cue–choice combinations, we found that rather than being generally cue-, choice-, or rule-selective, a large fraction of neurons in all imaged areas, but highest in RSC, showed increased activity specifically for a single trial type (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by selectivity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Neurons were selective for a specific cue–choice combination, which is consistent with nonlinear mixed selectivity.
source: Thus, neurons were selective for a specific cue–choice combination, which is consistent with a phenomenon often called nonlinear mixed selectivity (Fusi et al., 2016; Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the selectivity data with reference to the concept of mixed selectivity.

claim: Task complexity affected not only the necessity of cortical association areas for task performance but also their activity and selectivity levels.
source: In summary, we found increased activity and selectivity levels in RSC and PPC, but not V1, when comparing mice performing the switching task to mice performing the simple task. The relative increase was observed in both rules constituting the switching task, supported by mixed selectivity in single neurons. Thus, task complexity affected not only the necessity of cortical association areas for task performance as revealed in our photoinhibition experiments, but also their activity and selectivity levels.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the calcium imaging experiments comparing tasks.

claim: During the simple task, neurons in RSC and PPC had higher activity in mice with experience in the switching task than in mice trained only in the simple task.
source: Strikingly, during the simple task, neurons in RSC and PPC had higher activity in mice with experience in the switching task than in mice trained only in the simple task (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In mice with switching task experience, RSC and PPC neurons had higher average selectivity for the trial type and higher fractions of neurons with significant trial-type selectivity during the simple task.
source: Furthermore, in mice with switching task experience, RSC and PPC neurons had higher average selectivity for the trial type and higher fractions of neurons with significant trial-type selectivity (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The decoding of the trial type from population activity was more accurate in RSC and PPC in mice with complex-task experience during the simple task.
source: As a result, the decoding of the trial type from population activity was more accurate in these areas in mice with the complex-task experience (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Selectivity in V1 neurons was similar between mice with and without complex-task experience during the simple task.
source: Notably, selectivity in V1 neurons was similar between mice with and without complex-task experience.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 5C-E.

claim: The activity patterns of single neurons in PPC and RSC are strongly influenced not only by the current task performed, but also by previous task experience.
source: Therefore, the activity patterns of single neurons in PPC and RSC, including mean activity levels and selectivity, are strongly influenced not only by the current task performed, but also by previous task experience, mirroring the effect of previous task experience on the necessity of these areas for task performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing neural activity across training histories.

claim: The noise correlations within individual areas and across pairs of areas were lower on average in mice performing the switching task than in mice performing the simple task.
source: The noise correlations within individual areas and across pairs of areas were lower on average in mice performing the switching task than in mice performing the simple task (Figure 6A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by noise correlation analysis shown in Figures 6A-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Noise correlations were lower in mice with switching task experience compared to mice trained only in the simple task when performing the same simple task.
source: Strikingly, when we compared mice with different experience as they performed the same simple task, we also observed a difference in noise correlations both within and across cortical areas, with lower correlations in mice with switching task experience compared to mice trained only in the simple task (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by noise correlation analysis shown in Figures 6A-C.

claim: Mice with different task experience have significant differences in their population codes as they perform the same task.
source: Therefore, mice with different task experience have significant differences in their population codes as they perform the same task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the noise correlation analysis.

claim: The accuracy of decoding the trial type was slightly higher with correlations disrupted.
source: To reveal the impact of correlations on coding in our experiments, we disrupted noise correlations by shuffling trials of a given trial type separately for each neuron and repeated the trial-type decoding. The accuracy of decoding the trial type was slightly higher with correlations disrupted (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis with shuffled correlations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The lower correlations in mice performing the switching task or the simple task with switching task experience boosts information encoding along with higher trial-type selectivity levels.
source: Therefore, the lower correlations in mice performing the switching task or the simple task with switching task experience boosts information encoding along with higher trial-type selectivity levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation disruption analysis.

claim: The activity patterns in single neurons and neural populations are shaped by previous task experience.
source: Thus, these results reveal that the activity patterns in single neurons and neural populations are shaped by previous task experience.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Different sets of cortical areas and distinct neural activity patterns are utilized for the same task depending on an individual's training history.
source: Together, our findings demonstrate that different sets of cortical areas and distinct neural activity patterns are utilized for the same task depending on an individual's training history.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from combining optogenetic and imaging results.

claim: The necessity of cortical areas depends on factors separate from the task itself.
source: Our central finding is that mice with enhanced cognitive experience due to previous training on complex tasks require PPC and RSC to perform a simple task, whereas in mice without this previous training, PPC and RSC are largely dispensable for performing the same, simple task. Thus, the necessity of cortical areas depends on factors separate from the task itself.
evidence: This is a central conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: The differential cortical involvement in the groups of mice with and without training on the complex tasks is likely due to cognitive experience instead of sensory or motor learning.
source: This resulted in tasks of varying complexity, but the maze shape, and thus behavioral outputs needed, and choice-informative cues were identical between the complex and simple tasks. Therefore, the differential cortical involvement in the groups of mice with and without training on the complex tasks is likely due to cognitive experience instead of sensory or motor learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental design controlling for sensory and motor factors.

claim: Studies of perceptual experience and motor learning have emphasized that cortical necessity for task performance decreases with experience.
source: Studies of perceptual experience and motor learning have emphasized that cortical necessity for task performance decreases with experience (Chowdhury and DeAngelis, 2008; Hwang et al., 2019; Kawai et al., 2015) but see Liu and Pack, 2017.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in the literature.

claim: We found an increased necessity of cortical association areas due to cognitive experience in two distinct, complex tasks.
source: Instead, we found an increased necessity of cortical association areas due to cognitive experience in two distinct, complex tasks (delay and switching tasks).
evidence: This contrasts with previous findings and is supported by the optogenetic data.

claim: Earlier works did not identify differences in neural tuning in MT with perceptual experience despite differences in necessity.
source: In addition, these earlier works did not identify differences in neural tuning in MT with perceptual experience despite differences in necessity, leading to the proposal that differences in cortical necessity with experience arise from whether an area's activity is read out by a downstream network.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in the literature.

claim: Studies comparing various behavioral tasks with distinct levels of cortical necessity reported differences in neural activity across tasks.
source: On the other hand, studies comparing various behavioral tasks with distinct levels of cortical necessity reported differences in neural activity across tasks (Harvey et al., 2012; Pinto et al., 2019), suggesting that differences in cortical necessity may result from differential neural activity in the same areas.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in the literature.

claim: We found differences in neural activity depending not only on current task complexity, but also on training history.
source: Here, we did find differences in neural activity depending not only on current task complexity, but also on training history.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging experiments.

claim: During the same task, mice with complex training experience had higher selectivity in single neurons and weakened neuron–neuron correlations, compared to mice without this experience.
source: During the same task, mice with complex training experience had higher selectivity in single neurons and weakened neuron–neuron correlations, compared to mice without this experience, which together allowed for easier decoding of the relevant information from a population of neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data comparing training histories.

claim: These areas already contained high amounts of task-relevant information in the simple task without complex-task experience, contrasting the small performance deficits from inhibiting these areas in the same condition.
source: However, these areas already contained high amounts of task-relevant information in the simple task without complex-task experience, contrasting the small performance deficits from inhibiting these areas in the same condition.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing imaging and inhibition results.

claim: Although the boost in neural selectivity with complex-task experience increases the encoded information, it appears unlikely to be the sole reason for the large increase in cortical necessity for task performance.
source: Therefore, although the boost in neural selectivity with complex-task experience increases the encoded information, it appears unlikely to be the sole reason for the large increase in cortical necessity for task performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing imaging and inhibition results.

claim: Increased cortical necessity may result from a combination of increases in task information, reshaped representations of information, and/or modifications to information readouts.
source: Rather, increased cortical necessity may result from a combination of increases in task information, reshaped representations of information, and/or modifications to information readouts (Ruff and Cohen, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with reference to a theoretical framework.

claim: Cortical association areas had higher selectivity in their neural activity and were more strongly required for the complex tasks than the simple task.
source: We found that cortical association areas had higher selectivity in their neural activity and were more strongly required for the complex tasks than the simple task.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from both imaging and inhibition experiments.

claim: This finding supports the notion that cortex is needed for cognitively more challenging tasks.
source: This finding supports the notion that cortex is needed for cognitively more challenging tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of task complexity.

claim: The insertion of a delay period or of frequent association switches caused large increases in PPC necessity.
source: Indeed, the insertion of a delay period or of frequent association switches caused large increases in PPC necessity.
evidence: This is supported by the optogenetic inhibition data.

claim: PPC was necessary not only in the delay period but also in the cue period in the delay task.
source: In the delay task, PPC was necessary not only in the delay period but also in the cue period, possibly due to additional top-down attentional signals in the delay task relative to the simple task (Freedman and Ibos, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by segment-specific inhibition data with interpretation.

claim: PPC activity was dispensable in the intertrial interval following rule switches in the switching task.
source: In the switching task, PPC activity was dispensable in the intertrial interval following rule switches, when previous cues, choices, and outcomes are likely combined to update rule beliefs.
evidence: This is supported by ITI inhibition data.

claim: PPC may be especially important not for the combination of sensory cues with internal signals alone, but for their transformation into actions.
source: Thus, PPC may be especially important not for the combination of sensory cues with internal signals alone, but for their transformation into actions, consistent with strong encoding of ongoing movement in this area (Minderer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with reference to previous work.

claim: Inhibition of RSC had an intermediate effect on performance even in the simple task.
source: In contrast to PPC, inhibition of RSC had an intermediate effect on performance even in the simple task, in line with previous work on RSC supporting spatial navigation in general by relating egocentric sensory cues to allocentric positional information (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2015; Fischer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition data with reference to previous work.

claim: Larger RSC involvement in complex tasks was unlikely due to increased difficulty of navigating the visual scenery itself.
source: However, like for PPC, inhibiting RSC caused larger deficits when navigation was embedded in complex tasks. In those cases, because the navigation and visual components of a trial were identical across tasks, larger RSC involvement was unlikely due to increased difficulty of navigating the visual scenery itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental design and inhibition results.

claim: RSC plays a crucial role in cognitive aspects of navigation decisions, integrating visual cues flexibly with memory signals to plan navigational routes or choices.
source: These results support the emerging view that RSC plays a crucial role in cognitive aspects of navigation decisions, integrating visual cues flexibly with memory signals to plan navigational routes or choices (Franco and Goard, 2021; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Stacho and Manahan-Vaughan, 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with reference to emerging views in the literature.

claim: The long-lasting effect of cognitive experience on the necessity of PPC and RSC has important implications for the experimental study of cortical involvement in decision tasks.
source: The long-lasting effect of cognitive experience on the necessity of PPC and RSC has important implications for the experimental study of cortical involvement in decision tasks.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Many studies test an area's involvement or activity patterns in a single task and develop interpretations of an area's functions by extrapolating across studies.
source: Many studies, including our previous work, test an area's involvement or activity patterns in a single task and develop interpretations of an area's functions by extrapolating across studies (Lyamzin and Benucci, 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about common practices in the field.

claim: It seems critical to report the full details of how animals were trained on a task and what previous experiences they encountered.
source: Because prior task expertise can have a large effect on the involvement of cortical areas, it seems critical to report the full details of how animals were trained on a task and what previous experiences they encountered, both of which are commonly omitted from publications.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Increased PPC and RSC involvement relative to mice lacking complex-task experience is unlikely to stem from differences in task exposure times.
source: Increased PPC and RSC involvement relative to mice lacking complex-task experience is unlikely to stem from differences in task exposure times.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on analysis of training times and comparison to other studies.

claim: For mice with complex-task experience, the simple task did not present an unfamiliar challenge but was a simplification of a well-known task.
source: Importantly, our experimental design meant that for mice with complex-task experience, the simple task did not present an unfamiliar challenge but was a simplification of a well-known task.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: Simple task performance on trials without cortical silencing was similarly high in mice with and without complex-task experience.
source: Simple task performance on trials without cortical silencing was similarly high in mice with and without complex-task experience, suggesting that all groups of mice found the simple task similarly easy.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral performance data.

claim: This represents an interesting dissociation between cortical necessity and apparent task difficulty.
source: In contrast to comparisons across tasks of varying complexity, this represents an interesting dissociation between cortical necessity and apparent task difficulty.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Learning of the cue–choice associations in the complex tasks may create a network that is then used for the same associations in the simple task, with PPC and RSC as essential nodes.
source: We speculate that learning of the cue–choice associations in the complex tasks may create a network that is then used for the same associations in the simple task, with PPC and RSC as essential nodes that cannot be readily disengaged even when task complexity decreases.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: This reliance on association areas for simple task performance may equip animals with the capacity to quickly adjust behaviorally should the task complexity increase again.
source: This reliance on association areas for simple task performance may equip animals with the capacity to quickly adjust behaviorally should the task complexity increase again.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance.

claim: Mice previously trained on the switching task could still perform the switching task after 2 weeks of only simple task exposure.
source: This idea is supported by the fact that mice previously trained on the switching task could still perform the switching task after 2 weeks of only simple task exposure.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is unlikely that mice had to undergo substantial learning to perform the simple task after transitioning from a complex task.
source: However, we note that in our case, the cue–choice associations in the simple task were identical to those learned previously in the complex tasks for mice with experience in the delay or switching tasks. Thus, it is unlikely that mice had to undergo substantial learning to perform the simple task after transitioning from a complex task, which was supported by high behavioral performance in even the first session in the simple task after this transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental design and behavioral data.

claim: The cortical implementation of a task flexibly depends on initial conditions, as defined by past experience, and the overall optimization goal for the animal.
source: Together, our results indicate that the cortical implementation of a task flexibly depends on initial conditions, as defined by past experience, and the overall optimization goal for the animal, which in many cases is not just a single task but also previous tasks or other tasks occurring in parallel (Golub et al., 2018; Sadtler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a broad conclusion with reference to related concepts in the literature.

claim: These results highlight the tremendous flexibility of the brain to perform outwardly identical tasks using distinct sets of brain areas and neural activity patterns.
source: These results highlight the tremendous flexibility of the brain to perform outwardly identical tasks using distinct sets of brain areas and neural activity patterns and raise exciting challenges for understanding neural computation in the framework of dynamic and distinct neural solutions for a given cognitive problem.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion about the implications of the findings.

claim: Understanding cognitive processes will require considering the wider set of functions an animal is trying to optimize, beyond the computation of interest in a particular study.
source: We propose that understanding cognitive processes will require considering the wider set of functions an animal is trying to optimize, beyond the computation of interest in a particular study.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: To understand how long-ago cognitive experience and current cognitive demands set up different neural circuit landscapes, we suggest to carefully control for and to intentionally vary cognitive experience in laboratory settings.
source: To understand how long-ago cognitive experience and current cognitive demands set up these different neural circuit landscapes for outwardly identical navigation decisions, we suggest to carefully control for and to intentionally vary cognitive experience in laboratory settings (Plitt and Giocomo, 2021; Sharpe et al., 2021), thereby approximating more naturalistic scenarios.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation with references to related work.

claim: All optogenetic inhibition data were acquired from 19 male VGAT-ChR2-YFP mice.
source: All optogenetic inhibition data were acquired from 19 male VGAT-ChR2-YFP mice (The Jackson Laboratory, stock 014548).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: All calcium imaging data were acquired from six C57BL/6J-Tg (Thy1-GCaMP6s) GP4.3Dkim/J mice of both sexes.
source: All calcium imaging data were acquired from six C57BL/6J-Tg (Thy1-GCaMP6s) GP4.3Dkim/J mice (stock 024275) of both sexes (five females, one male).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Mice were 11–32 weeks old at the start of behavioral training.
source: Mice were 11–32 weeks old at the start of behavioral training.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Age at training start did not vary systematically across tasks.
source: Age at training start did not vary systematically across tasks (simple task: 21 ± 7 weeks (n = 7), switching task: 17 ± 5 weeks (n = 13), delay task: 21 ± 11 weeks (n = 5), mean ± standard deviation (SD), including photoinhibition and calcium imaging mice).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.
